newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Water firms eyed for shareholder benefits.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Water firms eyed for shareholder benefits.

text.p: British water companies Severn Trent and Yorkshire should squeeze half year profits higher when they report next week but the focus will be on any plans to give shareholders benefits, analysts said.

Severn Trent should turn in interim pretax profits of 193 to 210 million stg, up from 189 million stg previously, when it reports on Tuesday, with a dividend payout of 10.4 to 10.6 pence per share, compared with 9.20 pence.
It may announce some exceptional costs associated with its proposed bid for South West Water, which was blocked by the government in October.

Yorkshire's half year results on Friday November 29 should show pretax profits of 105 to 110 million stg compared with 99.5 million stg previously and a dividend payout increase to between 10.1 and 11.5 pence from 9.10 pence previously.

Both companies are being watched to see if they will offer shareholders either a special dividend or a share buyback, though the latter is considered less likely after recent changes to UK taxation. "If Yorkshire does not indicate some kind of balance sheet restructuring, the market could react quite belligerently," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.

Yorkshire, slammed by the media and penalised by industry regulator Ofwat with price curbs for failing to handle last year's drought adequately, has said it will not look at buybacks until customer confidence has been regained.
"Some people said that could take the company ten years but the market is hoping we are talking months," said the analyst.
New management, which took over in March, has stemmed the adverse criticism and analysts will be watching for further plans, particularly progress on its non-core business.

As a wave of speculation washes over the electricity sector after two recent bids, Yorkshire is also being watched for any indications it might be talking to local electricity company Yorkshire Electricity, analysts said.
Two combined utilities already exist and have secured attractive cost savings, United Utilities and Hyder.
Severn Trent will also be expected to return value to shareholders after the government blocked its bid for South West Water in October, along with a rival plan from Wessex Water.
But one analyst warned that Severn Trent managing director Vic Cocker might turn his attention to growing the business rather than giving large benefits to shareholders.
"The potential for a large special dividend or a buyback might not be as high as some think," he said.
Severn Trent is also expected to give some indications on progress at its waste management group Biffa, which one analyst felt could be close to contributing to profits after interest.

It might consider expansions in this area now its planned link-up with South West Water has been scuppered, analysts said, especially as its own local electricity company, East Midlands, agreed to a $1.3 billion bid from U.S.-based Dominion Resources on November 13.
